questions.text: What is a lifetime in the context of Rust references?

answers.text: The region in which a reference remains valid
The number of bytes occupied by a reference
The execution time of a function in milliseconds
The number of owners of a value

questions.explanation: Lifetimes describe reference validity and help the compiler prevent references to data that has already been destroyed.

Prevent dangling references
Describe relationships among the lifetimes of multiple references
Automatically extend local values until the end of the program

questions.text: Why does code with a reference `r` to a local variable `x` fail to compile when `x` goes out of scope before `r`?

Because `i32` values cannot be referenced
Because references must always be mutable
Because `println!` does not accept references

questions.explanation: The borrow checker compares scopes and rejects a reference that would outlive the data it points to.

Both strings must exist until the end of the program
`x` and `y` must refer to the same object
The function always returns `y`

`String::as_str` always returns an owned `String`

Because `&str` is forbidden as a return type

questions.text: What are lifetime elision rules?

A runtime memory-release mechanism

questions.text: How is the first lifetime elision rule stated?

answers.text: Each reference parameter gets its own lifetime
All input references always get one shared lifetime
Every output gets `static`
`self` never gets a lifetime

questions.text: How is the second lifetime elision rule stated?

answers.text: If there is exactly one input lifetime, it is assigned to every output reference
If there are two inputs, the longer one is chosen
Every output is always `static`
The result always receives the lifetime of `self`

questions.explanation: A single input lifetime unambiguously determines the lifetime of returned references.

questions.text: Why does `fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str` compile without explicit lifetimes? Select all correct answers.

Because there is one input lifetime, the second rule assigns it to the output reference
After those rules, all relationships among references in the signature are determined
Because every `&str` automatically has `static` lifetime

questions.explanation: This is the classic example where the first two elision rules fully determine the relationship.
